Chapter 1: Growing Up and Searching for Belonging
You know, childhood really is a wild ride—full of little adventures, each one shaping who we become.
Picture a quiet town in New Mexico. There’s a boy there, restless and bursting with imagination. Even before he knew what it meant to have an audience, he felt that pull to the stage. The world around him? Pretty ordinary. School. Family dinners. The usual daily hum. But inside? There was always this urge—to create, to entertain, to be truly seen.
His parents noticed something special right away. While most kids spent afternoons kicking soccer balls or trading cards, their son was busy putting on puppet shows in the living room, or memorizing lines from his favorite TV shows. There was a genuine wonder in how he saw things—a feeling that, with the right stage, anything was possible.
School brought its own set of challenges. Sure, he loved being the center of attention—making classmates laugh, landing just the right joke to impress a teacher. But there was always that nagging sense of not quite fitting in. The rules for being popular? They felt confusing, almost random. So, he learned to navigate it all with humor and charm—his quick wit became both a shield and a way to invite others in.
That first taste of the spotlight came with school plays and local theater. Standing under those bright lights, hearing the applause—it just clicked. It wasn’t only about people watching him; it was about connecting, about making the audience feel something real. The stage became a safe place, where the awkwardness of daily life melted away and a new kind of confidence started to grow.
Now, back at home, his family cheered him on, but there was always a little bit of caution mixed in. They encouraged his creativity but worried about the ups and downs of chasing a dream in show business. There were plenty of talks about being responsible, about focusing on school, about not betting everything on a dream that might never come true. Even so, that need to perform, to be seen, was just too strong to ignore.
As he moved into adolescence, things got even more complicated. Friendships changed, interests drifted, and suddenly, questions about identity became front and center. There were moments he felt totally out of sync with everyone around him. Sometimes, it was just easier to play a part—to be the funny one, the entertainer—than to let his guard down.
But even in those tougher moments, a deeper sense of self began to take root. Slowly, he realized that being different wasn’t something to hide—it could actually be a real strength. Learning to accept himself took time, and honestly, it wasn’t always easy. But every laugh, every successful show, every honest connection with someone else, helped lay the groundwork for what was coming next.
Looking back, those early years weren’t just about memorizing lines or pulling off a magic trick. They were really about finding out what it means to belong, to be seen, and to own the parts of yourself that don’t fit into anyone else’s box. It’s funny—most of us don’t realize just how much our adult lives are shaped by those early choices. By the decision to keep showing up, to keep trying, even when we have no idea how things will turn out.
